While it is tempting to do the preliminary work using data extraction methods that have less overhead (e.g., downloading into Excel using pre-established data connections), often these data are compressed or averaged differently and can cause major performance discrepancies during the deployment stage. 3.4 Train Model With the prepared dataset, an ML model may be trained by conducting feature engineering and model selection. However, as ML models increase in complexity, the demand for data increases exponentially. Without proper constraints it is possible to overfit a model where a statistical measure of performance, like R2, suggests success but fails when presented with new data. Thus, it is important to reduce the model complexity whenever possible, including reducing the number of model inputs or predictors by feature selection or dimension reduction. In feature selection, important variables are identified based on their correlation with the model output (e.g., correlation coefficients, minimum Redundancy Maximum Relevance (mRMR)) or changes to model accuracy when added or removed (e.g., feed forward, permutation). In dimension reduction, the variation in the data is modeled such that the changes in the data can be expressed in fewer model predictors (e.g., principal component analysis (PCA)). Both approaches reduce the number of model inputs and consequently the number of ML model parameters to be fit. Given the relatively small datasets found in water treatment, this is incredibly important. Unfortunately, there is no single model type that performs ‘best’ for water treatment applications given the variation in processes and properties of the data collected. Therefore, it is common to explore many different model types, like those presented in Table 2-1. In general, statistical approaches assume certain properties about the data being modeled whereas traditional ML approaches do not require these assumptions be upheld for successful modeling. Statistical models are much less complex than ML models and therefore could be more stable in data-sparce environments. Modified multiple linear regression approaches, like ridge regression, lasso regression, and adaptive lasso, should be explored as a more simplistic baseline that can be easily programmed into SCADA systems. There are a few major categories of ML models explored in this work: neural networks, ensemble models (random forest, XGBoost, AdaBoost), and clustering or similarity approaches (k nearest neighbors, support vector machines). The specifics of these models are well documented elsewhere; we will emphasize here that multiple algorithm structures should be explored during model training to identify which performs best with a given dataset. 3.5 Deploy Model Deployment is the stage where ML models transition from theoretical constructs to integral components of the operational process. It involves integrating the model into a new or existing operational change workflow.
